p: What is known of Bana's ancestry and early life is reconstructed from his own words: the introductory verses attached to the Kadambari and the first two chapters, or ucchvasas, of the Harshacharita. He was born to Chitrabhanu and Rajadevi in the village of Pritikuta, in a Kanyakubja Brahmin family. His mother died early and left him in the care of his father, who married again and had two more sons.

His father died when Bana was fourteen. For a time he led a colourful, wandering life with his half-brothers, and afterwards he came back to his native village. There, on a summer day, he received a letter from Krishna, a cousin of Harsha, and went to meet the king, who was camping near the town of Manitara. Harsha received him at first with mock signs of anger and then showed him much favour. Bana became the court poet during Harsha's reign at Kanyakubja.

The Harshacharita, whose title means the deeds of Harsha, was Bana's first composition; its third chapter describes the circumstances in which he came to write it. It is considered the first Indian work that may be regarded as a historical biography and the beginning of historical poetic writing in Sanskrit, and it gives a vivid picture of life in the Indian countryside.

Bana died before he could finish the Kadambari, and his son Bhushanabhatta completed it. Two further works are attributed to him, the Chandikashataka and a drama, the Parvatiparinaya. A Sanskrit saying, Banochhistam jagatsarvam, holds that Bana described everything in the world and left nothing out. The Harshacharita was translated into English by E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1897.

notes: Short article (under 300 words of substance): two sections, at the minimum length.
Diacritics dropped to match the site's spelling (Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa -> Bhushanabhatta, Caṇḍikāśataka -> Chandikashataka, Pārvatīpariṇaya -> Parvatiparinaya; the article writes 'ucchāvasa').
The article calls Harsha 'Emperor'; I wrote 'king' once, following the existing entry.
The article does not gloss the meaning of the saying beyond 'Bana has described everything in this world and nothing is left'.
